newsitem.title: DUBAI: Dubai gold market looks to India monsoon recovery.
newsitem.headline: Dubai gold market looks to India monsoon recovery.

text.p: Traders in Dubai's downtown gold souk are looking for a recovery in gold demand from the Indian subcontinent in July, now that the monsoon season has started in earnest in India.
Traders said on Sunday heavy rainfall in India in the past week, coupled with low international gold prices, was a good sign for gold demand in the coming weeks.

"There has been a heavy monsoon and from the beginning of July we are looking for renewed demand in gold and silver from India," said a trader dominant in the bullion export business to the subcontinent.
"I see good demand in July and August because the farmers will then be cash rich with the harvest and seasonal wedding demand will begin again," he added.
India's June to September monsoon season is the prelude to the start of the country's main wedding season when imports from key supply markets, particularly Dubai, increase.
Traders said this week's floods in India's western state of Gujarat, in which more than 100 people are feared to have died, had kept business there closed for most of the week.

"Businesses have been closed and no-one has been going to work. Now that the sun is coming out people are back at work -- even though Sunday is a day off -- and there will be a gold shortage so trade will pick up," one said.

He said as state taxes or octroi in Gujarat were lower than those in some other states, including Maharashtra, Gujarat was an important entry point for gold imports. Demand delayed by the floods was expected to filter through this week.
Traders said Dubai's local retail jewellery market was quiet in the week, with the onset of the long hot Arabian summer keeping tourists away and sending expatriate workers home for their holidays.

The price of Dubai's benchmark Ten Tola bar was pulled down in the week by soft international bullion prices. Traders quoted the TT bar -- 3.746 ounces of 24 carat gold -- at 4,635 dirhams ($1,263) on Sunday, down from 4,672 dirhams ($1,273) a week earlier.

The gold price slumped to its lowest level in nearly 4-1/4 years on Friday afternoon under pressure from a stronger dollar and short selling by professionals. It was fixed at $336.55 an ounce in London on Friday -- its lowest level since April 1, 1993 of $336.35.
Gold was last quoted on Saturday at $335.00/335.50 an ounce, down from $337.75/338.25 last week.

Some Dubai traders predicted further weakness in international prices. "The next support is around $331/332 and then the market is headed for $325. The low price is giving good support to physical offtake," one said.
